title: Garden of Genetics
tagline: A monk in a garden uncovers the hidden code of life.

scenes.text: Brno, Moravia, 1856. A quiet Augustinian friar tends his garden, planting peas in careful rows. He is tracking seven traits — seed color, pod shape, plant height. Over eight years he will grow 29,000 pea plants and discover the laws governing all inheritance.

scenes.speaker: Gregor Mendel
scenes.text: Dominant and recessive. These two words contain the secret of heredity. Cross a tall plant with a short one — all the offspring are tall. But the shortness is hiding, not gone. In the next generation, it returns, one in four.

challenge.instruction: Cross two round-seeded hybrids and the wrinkled seeds come back. Breed the peas and find the proportion Mendel counted in the next generation.
challenge.fact: Mendel chose pea plants (Pisum sativum) with extraordinary care. They had clearly distinguishable traits — smooth or wrinkled seeds, yellow or green pods, tall or short stems — that produced consistent, countable offspring. Over eight years, he tracked 29,000 plants and applied mathematics to biology for the first time.

scenes.text: Mendel presented his findings in 1865. The scientific community ignored them for 35 years. When his work was rediscovered in 1900, it instantly became the foundation of genetics and, eventually, of molecular biology.

challenge.instruction: Mendel's 1865 lectures in Brno rested on counts no naturalist had bothered to make. Add up the tallies from his pea beds.
challenge.fact: When Mendel published his results in 1866, the scientific world largely ignored them. His paper was cited only a handful of times in the next 35 years. It was not until 1900 — 16 years after Mendel's death — that three botanists independently rediscovered his laws and finally found his original paper, launching the science of genetics.

scenes.speaker: Gregor Mendel
scenes.text: The garden is my laboratory. The pea is my instrument. I believe that what I have found in these plants applies to all living things — including the nature that makes humans different from one another. Future scientists will confirm this.

challenge.instruction: Mendel wrote of hidden 'elements' passed from parent to offspring; the next century gave them a five-letter name. Guess it.
challenge.fact: The 3:1 ratio Mendel observed — three dominant to one recessive — was not a coincidence or approximation. It was a mathematical law. Mendel was the first scientist to apply statistical analysis to biology, and his insight that inheritance comes in discrete packets (what we now call genes) was centuries ahead of its time.

scenes.text: Mendel tested every ratio the hard way: each cross repeated, each seed sorted and counted by hand.

challenge.instruction: Breed peas the way Mendel did, crossing plants or letting one pollinate itself. Plan each cross on a Punnett square, the grid Reginald Punnett drew in 1905 to explain results like Mendel's, before you spend a season on it.
challenge.fact: A Punnett square maps out all possible genetic combinations from two parents. When Mendel crossed round-seeded (Rr) plants together, the square predicts 25% RR, 50% Rr and 25% rr offspring: 75% round, 25% wrinkled. The 3:1 ratio that baffled naturalists for centuries was hiding in plain arithmetic.

challenge.instruction: Classify each pea plant trait as dominant or recessive — just as Mendel did in his monastery garden, sorting thousands of seeds by hand.
challenge.fact: Mendel identified seven distinct traits in pea plants, each with a dominant and recessive form. Remarkably, the genes controlling these seven traits happen to lie on different chromosomes, which is why Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment holds perfectly for them — a stroke of extraordinary scientific luck.

challenge.instruction: Eight years of counting go into print at last. Set the title of Mendel's paper for the Brünn society's Proceedings and pull a clean proof.
challenge.fact: Mendel kept records of extraordinary precision across eight years of experiments. He tracked 29,000 plants through multiple generations, recording results in tables that would not be out of place in a modern biology lab. His data was so clean that statistician R.A. Fisher later controversially suggested it was too perfect.

scenes.speaker: Gregor Mendel
scenes.text: This time the whole board is judged at once. Deploy Alan Turing, Mohandas Gandhi and me, turn us public, then declare the Expedition: the highest public Intelligence on the board when the round ends takes the prize.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 6 · Global Competition. Deploy your Great People, Go Public on each, then start the Expedition and End Turn to win the round with the highest public Intelligence on the board.
challenge.fact: A Global Competition counts every public Great Person on the whole board; followers and face-down cards add nothing. It lasts one round, and the strongest player draws a reward: event cards, followers or a new Great Person.
